newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Top Austrian banker raps political pressure.
newsitem.headline: Top Austrian banker raps political pressure.

text.p: One of Austria's most distinguished bankers said on Wednesday the country's banks remained subject to political pressure and urged the government to press ahead with privatising the financial sector.

"As long as government bodies own banks, there is necessarily a certain political pressure," Guido Schmidt-Chiari told Austrian state radio one day after he stepped down as chief executive of Austrian bank Creditanstalt.
"That's why it is essential to continue privatising as is the case in most other Western countries," he added.

His comments came amid mounting criticism of the state's involvement in Austria's banking system following the suicide at the weekend of Gerhard Praschak, board member of clearing house and export financing agency Kontrollbank (OeKB).
Before shooting himself in the head, Praschak sent reams of documents to opposition parties and state prosecutors, claiming his career was under threat due to political pressure.
The allegations centred around partly state-controlled Bank Austria, by far the country's biggest bank and the most powerful player in Austrian industry.
In his notes, Praschak claimed Bank Austria chief executive Gerhard Randa had been a key figure behind attempts to place ex-minister Rudolf Scholten on the OeKB board.
Praschak said he felt under pressure to make room for Scholten, who was appointed to the board last week.
Randa swiftly denied the allegations and told Austrian state television that the idea of using political pressure on banks to find jobs for ex-government officials was a cliche.

"(The reality) is different," he said. "The fact that the understanding of reality of somebody who is able to commit such an act is somewhat limited, doesn't make this cliche any truer," he added in reference to Praschak's notes.
Randa, closely linked to the ruling Social Democrats, chairs OeKB's supervisory board. Bank Austria is also OeKB's key customer, accounting for the lion's share of export financing in Austria.

Randa is also supervisory board chairman of Creditanstalt, which Bank Austria acquired in January, and president of Vienna's stock exchange, where the Bank Austria group controls some 80 percent of all trading activity.
Although the government sold its 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt to Bank Austria, the state's involvement in the banking sector remains pervasive.
The state effectively controls 19 percent of Bank Austria, while the majority of the bank's capital is held by the City of Vienna's AVZ foundation, chaired by Randa.
The government also effectively controls postal savings bank PSK, which ministers pledged partly to sell off this year.
And under a political agreement over the sale of Creditanstalt to Bank Austria, both the state and the City of Vienna will gradually withdraw from the bank over five years.
Austrian opposition parties have joined Schmidt-Chiari's calls for speeding up bank privatisations.
"The consequence of this affair has to be a withdrawal of politics from the banking sector. Privatisation of banks is the only answer," Liberal Forum leader Heide Schmidt said.
